grade.rationale: The helper is concise and generally clear, but its documented best-effort recording contract is not enforced, and its wrapper detection can misclassify unrelated JSON containing a usage property.

summary: Two issues merit attention: AdHocUsageRecorder exceptions can escape despite the stated never-throws contract, and ParseOrFallback recognizes a broader JSON shape than its comments describe. Focused unit tests around recorder failures and ambiguous JSON objects would improve confidence.

grade.rationale: Normal wrapper and plain-text paths appear sound, but objects with any top-level usage property can be incorrectly treated as Claude CLI wrappers.
The implementation is small and centralized, though wrapper-shape recognition duplicates an implicit external format contract and should be made stricter or encapsulated.
Names and documentation are helpful, but the implementation contradicts both the wrapper-shape explanation and the stated never-throws behavior.
Parsing degrades safely, but recording exceptions are not contained even though recording is explicitly documented as best-effort and non-throwing.
The stateless methods are easy to exercise, but direct UTC clock access prevents deterministic timestamp assertions and recorder-failure behavior needs explicit coverage.

findings.title: Record does not honor its never-throws contract
findings.description: The class documentation says recording is best-effort and never throws, but Record invokes recorder.Record without exception handling. If the recorder performs file or other fallible I/O, an observability failure can fail an otherwise successful ad-hoc operation.
findings.recommendation: Contain expected recorder exceptions inside Record and report them through an appropriate non-throwing diagnostic path. Add a test using a recorder that throws to verify that the caller remains unaffected. Avoid catching fatal runtime exceptions indiscriminately if the recorder exposes more specific failure types.

findings.title: Any top-level usage property is accepted as a CLI wrapper
findings.description: The detection predicate accepts either type equal to result or the mere presence of a usage property. This can misclassify domain JSON that happens to contain usage, contradicting the stated intent to treat non-wrapper JSON as plain text. It then passes that document to OrchestratorRunner.ParseResult and may replace the original content with an empty or incorrectly parsed reply.
findings.recommendation: Require the authoritative wrapper discriminator, such as a string type property equal to result, and validate any other required wrapper fields before parsing. If compatibility with a known legacy shape is required, recognize that shape explicitly and cover both ambiguous domain JSON and malformed wrappers with tests.

findings.title: Broad catch silently hides all parsing failures
findings.description: The catch block converts every exception from JSON parsing and OrchestratorRunner.ParseResult into a plain-text fallback without diagnostics. While fallback is appropriate for malformed or incompatible output, silently suppressing unexpected implementation failures makes regressions difficult to distinguish from legitimate non-wrapper input.
findings.recommendation: Catch expected JSON and wrapper-format exceptions specifically. If broader containment is required at this boundary, emit a non-throwing diagnostic that identifies the failure category without logging sensitive stdout.
